pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Sketch (or describe) a small binary tree and point out its root, a leaf, a subtree, one node's depth, and the tree's height. Then: what extra rule turns a binary tree into a BST?
expected_points: root has no parent, leaf has no children, any node plus everything below it is a subtree
depth counts edges from the root down; height counts edges on the longest path down to a leaf
BST rule: at every node, ALL keys in the left subtree are smaller and ALL keys in the right subtree are larger — whole subtrees, not just direct children

questions.prompt: Walk me through how your Insert finds where a new key belongs, and why the BST invariant still holds afterwards. What happens when the key is already in the tree?
expected_points: compare at each node and go left if smaller, right if larger — the same walk as search
the new node attaches at the empty spot where the walk falls off, so it lands on the correct side of every ancestor
returning the subtree root and re-attaching it (root.Left = Insert(...)) handles the empty case; an equal key changes nothing

questions.prompt: For the tree built from 5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 9: what do in-order, pre-order, and post-order produce, and what is each ordering good for?
expected_points: in-order: 1 3 4 5 7 8 9 — sorted, because left < node < right at every node
pre-order: 5 3 1 4 8 7 9 — root first; replaying it through insert rebuilds the same tree (copy/serialize)
post-order: 1 4 3 7 9 8 5 — children before parent; for tear-down or bottom-up computations

questions.prompt: Your BST holds the same 1023 keys in both runs of the height test, yet one tree has height 9 and the other 1022. Explain what happened and what it does to search cost.
expected_points: search and insert cost O(h), the height, because each step descends one level
sorted insertion always attaches to the right, producing a chain with h = n-1, so operations are O(n)
a balanced insertion order keeps levels full so h is about log2 n, giving O(log n); self-balancing BSTs enforce this regardless of input order

questions.prompt: One service only checks whether a session token exists; another lists events between two timestamps. For each: BST or hash table, and why?
expected_points: token existence: hash table — O(1) average exact lookup and ordering buys nothing
time-range listing: BST — keys stay ordered, so a range query is O(log n + matches) and results come out sorted
a hash table cannot do ranges without scanning all n keys, because hashing scatters the ordering

questions.prompt: Convince me that in-order traversal of ANY valid BST is sorted — not just for the tree in the exercise.
expected_points: at each node the invariant guarantees everything emitted before it (left subtree) is smaller and everything after (right subtree) is larger
the same argument applies recursively inside each subtree, so the whole output is ascending
corollary: an unsorted in-order output proves the invariant is broken somewhere

questions.prompt: Why does Height return -1 for the empty tree instead of 0? What breaks in the recursive definition if you pick 0?
expected_points: height is defined as 1 + max(height of children); a single node's children are empty trees
with empty = -1, a single node computes 1 + (-1) = 0 edges, which matches the definition
with empty = 0, a single node would claim height 1 and every height would be off by one (counting nodes, not edges)
